The blade shape and cooling hole configuration used were representative of actual gas turbine blades.
The ratio of boundary layer displacement thickness to hole diameter was approximately 0.09.
The ratio of coolant mass flux to mainstream mass flux (blowing rate, M) had values between 0.2 and 2.
Both the mainstream and coolant flows were turbulent in the experiments.
A heat-mass transfer analogy was used to determine film cooling effectiveness from concentration measurements.
The momentum flux ratio I cos^2(α) was found to be an important parameter describing the interaction between the coolant jet and mainstream.
For I cos^2(α) < 1, the film cooling effectiveness was up to twice as large on a convex wall and only half as large on a concave wall compared to a flat plate.
The effect of curvature was smaller for film cooling with two rows of holes compared to a single row.
Differences in film cooling effectiveness between previous studies were partly attributed to whether the coolant injection flow was laminar or turbulent.
The ratio of heat transfer coefficients with and without film cooling was close to 1 for X/D > 30 when the approaching boundary layer was turbulent.
Large gradients in local heat transfer coefficients, up to 7 times the two-dimensional value, were observed near the cooling holes.
